nameStory: The name 'boneset' comes from this plant's traditional use in folk medicine to treat 'breakbone fever' (dengue fever), where patients felt like their bones were breaking from severe aches and pains. The 'upland' part of its name distinguishes it from its wetland-loving cousin, common boneset, since this species prefers drier, higher ground. Early settlers and Native Americans brewed the bitter leaves into medicinal teas, though we don't recommend this today!
description: Upland boneset is a sturdy perennial wildflower that grows 2-4 feet tall in late summer. It produces clusters of small, fluffy white flowers that look like tiny puffs of cotton arranged in flat-topped bouquets at the stem tips. The plant has a somewhat weedy appearance with its rough, hairy stems and narrow leaves that attach directly to the stem without stalks. It's a member of the huge sunflower family, though its flowers look nothing like the classic daisy shape we might expect.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves that feel rough and sandpapery to the touch, arranged in opposite pairs directly attached to the stem with no leaf stalks - this 'sessile' attachment gives the plant its scientific name

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense, flat-topped clusters of tiny white flowers that look like miniature cotton balls or shaving cream, each individual flower head containing only 5 small disc flowers with no petals

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright, somewhat scraggly-looking plant reaching 2-4 feet tall with multiple branching stems that feel distinctly hairy and rough when you run your fingers along them

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Fluffy white seed heads in fall that blow apart like dandelion seeds, each tiny seed equipped with a parachute of silky white hairs

habitat: Look for upland boneset in dry, open areas like fields, meadows, roadsides, and woodland edges throughout New England. Unlike its wetland-loving relative common boneset, this species prefers well-drained soils and can handle some drought. It often grows alongside goldenrods, asters, and other late-summer wildflowers in sunny to partially shaded spots.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as fuzzy, reddish shoots from underground roots. Young leaves are noticeably hairy and rough-textured even when small.
seasonality.summer: Plant reaches full height by midsummer and begins forming flower buds in late July. The distinctive opposite, stalkless leaves are most obvious during active growing season.
seasonality.fall: Blooms from August through September with dense white flower clusters, followed by fluffy seed heads that persist and disperse on autumn winds.
seasonality.winter: Dried brown stems may persist with some remaining seed head remnants, though the plant dies back to underground roots.

funFact: Despite being called 'boneset,' this plant actually contains compounds that can be toxic to the liver if consumed in large quantities - the opposite of the healing properties early settlers believed it possessed!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with common boneset, but upland boneset has narrow leaves that don't wrap around the stem, while common boneset has distinctive leaves that are joined together around the stem like a cup. Memory trick: 'upland' has narrow leaves that don't wrap, while 'common' has leaves that connect completely around the stem.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name 'sessilifolium' literally means 'sitting leaves' in Latin, referring to how the leaves sit directly on the stem without leaf stalks. This is actually the most reliable way to distinguish it from other bonesets, making the scientific name unusually helpful for field identification.
compareHints: Among the many boneset species, upland boneset is distinguished by its narrow, stalkless leaves that don't wrap around the stem like common boneset, and its preference for dry habitats unlike most other bonesets. It's smaller and less robust than late boneset, and lacks the extremely narrow, linear leaves of hyssopleaf thoroughwort. The combination of rough, opposite leaves without stalks and dry habitat preferences makes it fairly distinctive in the genus.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Eupatorium relatives, common boneset is the only one with perfoliate leaves where the stem pierces through the leaf base.

Among the bonesets, hyssopleaf thoroughwort stands out immediately for its extremely narrow leaves—while common boneset has broad, wrinkled leaves that clasp the stem, and rough boneset has lance-shaped leaves, this species looks almost grass-like.

Among the boneset family, rough boneset stands out for its notably hairy, rough-textured leaves and stems, while common boneset has distinctive leaves that appear "perforated" by the stem passing through them.
Among the boneset family, late boneset stands out for its very late bloom time and alternate leaf arrangement.
Unlike common boneset which has leaves that appear to be pierced by the stem, New England boneset has clearly separate opposite leaves.
Among the boneset family, tall boneset stands out with its alternate leaf arrangement (most other bonesets have opposite leaves) and its particularly dense, flat-topped flower clusters.
Among its boneset relatives, roundleaf thoroughwort is the wetland specialist with the roundest, softest leaves.
Among its boneset relatives in New England, dogfennel is unmistakable due to its incredibly fine, thread-like leaves - all other Eupatorium species have broad, simple leaves.
Hemp agrimony stands out immediately from all native New England Eupatorium species because of its deeply divided, palm-shaped leaves – every other boneset in our region has simple, undivided leaves.
Unlike common boneset which has distinctive perfoliate leaves that appear to be pierced by the stem, Torrey's eupatorium has narrow, separate leaves.
Unlike common boneset with its perforated leaves that wrap around the stem, veined thoroughwort has clearly separate opposite leaves.
